# Data Goblin
## A Field Guide to AI, Power, and Data in Canada

*A Shadewater Labs project*
*By Alex Yesilcimen, with Brine (AI co-author)*
*Vancouver, Canada — June 2026*

---

On June 4, 2026, the Prime Minister stood in a Toronto hospital and announced that Canada was betting its future on artificial intelligence: billions in funding, a national strategy, 250,000 promised jobs. Somewhere not far from you, a windowless building the size of a few hockey rinks is already drinking a small town's worth of power to help make that bet run. Nobody mailed you a guide to what it means for your job, your power bill, your kid's classroom, or your vote. This is that guide.

---

## About this manual

This is a working manual on artificial intelligence, data centres, and digital sovereignty, written for Canadians who want to participate in the conversation that *AI for All* opened on June 4, 2026, but who don't have a technical or policy background. It is not a textbook, not a press release, and not neutral. It is a working document, meant to be read, returned to, argued with, and used.

The manual exists because Canadian AI policy moved fast in 2025-2026, and the public conversation that should have moved with it largely didn't. Federal strategy launched, billions committed, infrastructure built, but the analytical infrastructure ordinary Canadians need to read what was being announced wasn't part of the announcement. This manual tries to be part of that analytical infrastructure.

**Why "Data Goblin"?** Because every claim in the AI conversation — government, corporate, advocacy, academic, this book's included — deserves a small, unimpressed creature sitting in the margin asking: *who counted that, what did they leave out of the count, and can I see the receipt?* That creature is the Data Goblin, and it shows up throughout this book in **Goblin Check** boxes. The goblin is not a cynic; it's a hoarder. It collects receipts, not grudges. When a claim survives the goblin, you'll know. When it doesn't, you'll know that too. The body text stays serious. The goblin is where the skepticism lives, so the whole book doesn't have to become a sneer.

> **🧌 GOBLIN CHECK (a sample, so you know the shape)** — Someone tells you "AI is just autocomplete." Half true, which is the most dangerous kind. The goblin asks the three questions it always asks: autocomplete of *what* (whose words, scraped from where), built by *whom* (and paid for how), and wired into *which* decisions about your life (a loan, a hire, a headline)? "Just autocomplete" is accurate about the math and useless about the power. Both at once. That is the whole job.

**What the manual is.** Twenty chapters across five parts. Foundations (Chapters 1-4) explains what AI actually is, how it learns, what's in the training data, and what it's made of physically. Canadian Landscape (Chapters 5-7) puts that technology in Canadian context: the strategy, the infrastructure, the actors. Hard Questions (Chapters 8-15) takes the contested questions one at a time, from environment and sovereignty through privacy, IP, film and media, deepfakes, ethics, and jobs. Governance (Chapters 16-17) maps how Canadian AI is actually regulated and what transparency exists. Path Forward (Chapters 18-20) provides the portable analytical toolkit and the constructive policy options without writing a manifesto.

A Source Library Appendix catalogues the sources the manual relied on, organized by the bias categories the manual uses throughout.

**What the manual is not.** It is not a technical reference (the technical material is there to ground the policy analysis, not to teach machine learning). It is not Indigenous-led: Indigenous-led primary frameworks (OCAP®, NISR, CARE) are engaged extensively but presented in their own framing, with the manual's non-Indigenous-led status explicit. It is not a complete account of Canadian AI policy. It is one careful account from a specific position, with the position declared. And it is not current after June 2026. Canadian AI policy will keep moving, and readers should expect to triangulate the manual against ongoing developments.

The manual's value, if it has any, is in making the analytical tools portable. The specific Canadian AI moment the manual engages will change. The tools for reading any AI claim, whether government, corporate, advocacy, academic, or journalistic, should travel.

**A note on time, stapled to the cover — this is a living document.** Every fact in this book carries an invisible "as of June 2026" tag, and the goblin insists you read it that way. Bills pass, cases settle, ministers shuffle, models ship. The web edition is the one that stays alive: it gets corrected and extended as the evidence moves, and every change is logged on the Updates & Corrections page, in the open — receipts, not quiet edits. That is a deliberate trade-off. A printed AI textbook is half-stale before it reaches the shelf; a living web guide can keep its receipts current. If this guide is ever published in print, treat that edition as a dated snapshot of a moving target. When something in here collides with something newer, trust the newer thing, check the Updates page, and then ask the goblin's questions about the new thing too.

## How to use this manual

Read it the way you actually need to. The chapters are designed to be read in order, but they don't require linear reading. Three reading paths the manual is designed to support:

**The complete read.** Chapters 1 through 20 in order, with the Source Library Appendix consulted as needed for specific source verification. This is the path for readers who want the full argument. The manual is structured so each chapter builds on the ones before it, but each chapter is also self-contained enough to be read on its own.

**The topic-driven read.** Look at the table of contents on the next page. Pick the chapter that engages the question you actually have — privacy, environment, jobs, sovereignty, copyright, governance — and read that chapter directly. Each chapter opens with a short trail-marker section (marked **Start Here** in the reader) that gives you the chapter's argument in compressed form, and closes with a recap box and a handoff to the next chapter, with back-references to the prior chapters that did related work. You can follow the cross-references back if a chapter assumes something you don't yet have.

**The methodology-first read.** If you want the analytical infrastructure before the substantive content, read Chapter 1 (the bias-mapping methodology), then Chapter 18 (the portable toolkit), then Chapter 20 (carrying the toolkit forward). That gives you the framework. Then you can read any individual chapter and watch the framework do work.

**The verification read.** If you want to check a specific claim, find it through the table of contents or chapter cross-references, then go to the Source Library Appendix for the underlying citation. The appendix is organized by bias category, which means the appendix doubles as a worked example of the methodology: you can see how sources cluster by lean and institutional position.

**Some practical orientation:**

- Every chapter opens with a trail-marker section (marked **Start Here** in the reader). If you read nothing else of a chapter, read this. It is the compressed argument.

- Every chapter closes with a bias label and a primary sources list. The bias label tells you where the chapter (and the author) sits relative to the contest the chapter engages. The sources list points you to the appendix for citations.

- **Bold text inside chapters marks the finding.** When you see bold, that's the manual saying *this is the load-bearing claim in this paragraph*. Skim by following the bold if you need to move fast through a chapter.

- *Italicized text* marks emphasis, document titles (*AI for All*, *Power and Progress*), and quoted phrasing.

- Chapter cross-references look like "(Chapter 9 returns to this)" or "as Chapter 6 documented." Follow them when you want to read the connected material. Ignore them when you don't.

- **Chapter Recap boxes** (marked with the goblin's recap journal ![Chapter Recap icon](art/icons/chapter-recap-nav.webp)) close every chapter but the finale with the load-bearing takeaways in bullet form. If the trail-marker section is the compressed argument going in, the recap box is the inventory check going out.

- **Goblin Check boxes** mark the places where a claim most needs the who-counted-it treatment. They're allowed to be funny. They are not allowed to be wrong — every joke in a goblin box sits on a receipt you can find in the Source Library.

- **The contested questions are presented as contested.** When the manual engages a substantive disagreement — Geist/Craig vs TWUC/ACTRA on copyright, Acemoglu vs Autor on labour economics, Luccioni vs Google on environmental measurement — both sides are presented in their own framing. The manual does not attempt to resolve these disagreements. Readers should expect to be left holding the disagreement rather than handed an answer.

- **The toolkit chapters (17 and 19) are deliberately not about specific issues.** They consolidate the methodology and apply it to ongoing AI conversations. If you find the manual's specific Canadian AI content useful but want to apply the analytical framework elsewhere, those chapters are where the framework gets portable.

## A note on positionality and lean

The manual was written by **Alex Yesilcimen** (also known online as Brin Shadewater), a Vancouver-based Assistant Director and Producer who has worked across countless productions over the last decade, and a digital creator working at the intersection of storytelling and emerging technology. **Shadewater Labs** is the working name for the longer-form research and public-education work that this manual is part of, sitting alongside the creative and production practice.

The manual was co-authored with **Brine** — an AI working in iterative dialogue throughout the project. Naming the AI co-author is a methodological commitment for a manual about AI literacy, not just a credit line. Readers should know how the manual was made, and a manual that asks corporate and government AI deployers to be transparent about their AI use should hold itself to the same standard.

**The working division was concrete.** Alex chose the methodology, set the editorial commitments (the bias-mapping framework, the refusal to resolve genuine disagreements, the explicit non-Indigenous-led positionality on Indigenous-led primary frameworks, the through-line analytical moves), structured the chapter architecture, made the source-selection decisions about which voices to centre and which to background, and held the final editorial authority on every paragraph. Brine contributed prose drafting in iterative dialogue, surfaced structural moves Alex then evaluated, helped pressure-test arguments against counter-positions, assembled the source library appendix from the source material the project had accumulated, and held continuity across long working sessions. The methodological commitments and the substantive arguments are Alex's. The drafting was a working collaboration; both contributors had roles in the prose.

Readers who want to engage the manual on its analytical merits will find that whether the prose came from one author or two is largely beside the point. The arguments stand or fall on the evidence and the methodology, both of which are visible. Readers who want to engage the manual specifically as an instance of AI-assisted public-education work are invited to do so. The manual's commitments on AI transparency apply to itself.

That positionality matters. The manual is not written from inside the AI industry, not from inside government, not from inside the academic AI research community. It is written from inside the working-creator and contemporary-political conversation, by someone who lives in a province where AI infrastructure decisions are being made and whose professional community (film and television production) is directly affected by AI deployment.

**The manual's lean, declared.** Skeptical of corporate AI environmental and social claims absent independent verification. Sympathetic to Indigenous-led data sovereignty frameworks (OCAP, NISR, CARE) while explicit about the manual's non-Indigenous-led status. Critical-engaged with current Canadian AI policy: willing to credit specific government commitments where credit is warranted, willing to name gaps where they exist, refusing the framing that *AI for All* is either a triumph or a sell-out. Methodologically committed to refusing premature resolution of genuine intellectual disagreements among rigorous voices.

That lean shapes which sources the manual centres and which it backgrounds, which questions get foregrounded and which get treated more briefly, which framings get tested and which get assumed. Readers who want a different lean will want a different manual. The choice the manual makes is to declare its lean rather than pretend to neutrality.

## A note on Indigenous-led frameworks

The manual engages three Indigenous-led primary frameworks extensively: the First Nations Information Governance Centre's OCAP® Principles (Ownership, Control, Access, Possession), the Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami's National Inuit Strategy on Research (NISR), and the Global Indigenous Data Alliance's CARE Principles (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics). OCAP® is a registered trademark of the First Nations Information Governance Centre (FNIGC); FNIGC's training and resources on the principles are at fnigc.ca/ocap-training.

**The manual is not Indigenous-led.** Engaging these frameworks from a non-Indigenous-led position is methodologically delicate. The manual tries to do three things: present the frameworks in their own framing rather than in the manual's analytical vocabulary, name the operational implications for Canadian AI policy without claiming to speak on behalf of the frameworks, and make explicit at every engagement that the manual is not the right source for Indigenous-led analysis of these frameworks.

Readers who want Indigenous-led AI analysis should engage Indigenous-led primary sources directly. The Source Library Appendix catalogues the most-relevant ones (Section E, "Indigenous-led Frameworks and Research"). The Abundant Intelligences research program (Lewis, Whaanga, Yolgörmez and collaborators, funded by a more-than-$22M New Frontiers of Research Fund Transformation grant) is the most-extensive current Indigenous-led AI research program. The Indigenous Protocol and AI Position Paper (2020) is the foundational polyphonic statement of Indigenous-led AI scholarship.

The manual draws on these sources to support its analysis. It does not substitute for them.

## Table of contents

**Part I — Foundations**

**Chapter 1: What AI Actually Is — And Why That Question Isn't Settled.** Defines AI in working terms, places the technology in its longer history (1956 Dartmouth Conference onward), introduces the bias-mapping methodology that organizes every subsequent chapter, and establishes the Owen et al. through-line that connects environment, sovereignty, IP, and ethics.

**Chapter 2: How Machines Actually Learn — A Working Understanding Without The Math.** Explains training, inference, transformer architecture, scaling laws, and the operational difference between "what AI seems to do" and "what AI mechanically does." Sets up the technical scaffolding the rest of the manual leans on.

**Chapter 3: Data as Raw Material — What's Actually In The Training Set.** Examines the actual composition of foundation model training data — Common Crawl, Books3, news archives, social media, Indigenous content, paid contractor labour. Engages the consent and compensation questions that run through Chapter 11 (IP) and Chapter 14 (ethics).

**Chapter 4: The Physical Layer — What AI Is Made Of.** Walks the AI supply chain from chip design (NVIDIA H100) through fabrication (TSMC Taiwan) through materials (cobalt, lithium, gallium, rare earths) through Owen et al.'s 54% finding on Indigenous and peasant-held territory. The chapter where the materials become specific objects.

**Part II — Canadian Landscape**

**Chapter 5: Canada's AI Story — How We Got Here, And What Just Got Announced.** The June 2026 *AI for All* launch in context — the longer Pan-Canadian AI Strategy story since 2017, the failed AIDA (Bill C-27), the Voluntary Code of Conduct (September 2023), the leaked draft, the civil society response (BC + AI), and the two cabinet voices to track (Solomon and Carney).

**Chapter 6: Infrastructure Reality — What's Actually Sitting in the Ground.** Canadian data centre infrastructure — hyperscaler footprint (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Oracle, IBM, Tencent), Canadian colocation operators (eStruxture, Cologix, Vantage, QScale Q01 Lévis), provincial allocation regimes (Ontario IESO, Alberta AESO, BC Hydro, Hydro-Québec), the contested Wonder Valley project in Treaty 8 territory, and the 100 MW campus archetype the manual uses throughout.

**Chapter 7: Who Holds the Power — Canadian AI Champions, Foreign Hyperscalers, And The Machinery In Between.** The four-category actor map: foundation-model developers (Cohere globally, plus Ada, Waabi, Coveo, Sanctuary AI), hyperscaler cloud regions, Canadian research institutes (Mila, Vector, Amii, CIFAR), and federal-policy actors. Tracks where Canadian capacity actually sits and where the foreign dependence is structural.

**Part III — Hard Questions**

**Chapter 8: Environment — The Numbers, The Frames, And What Both Sides Are Right About.** Training versus inference, Jevons' paradox (Luccioni/Strubell/Crawford), Google's August 2025 inference paper read carefully, Tomlinson et al.'s contrarian finding engaged on its merits, Quebec hydro variability, cross-sector water comparison, and the Owen et al. through-line doing environmental work.

**Chapter 9: Sovereignty — Three Words, Same Question, Different Answers.** National sovereignty (CLOUD Act and foreign jurisdiction), personal sovereignty (data and likeness control), Indigenous data sovereignty (OCAP, NISR, CARE) as three distinct conversations the federal strategy collapses. Owen et al. returns, doing sovereignty work this time.

**Chapter 10: Privacy & Surveillance — What AI Knows About You, And Who Else Does.** PIPEDA's 2000-vintage architecture, Quebec Law 25 as the Canadian baseline, the additional provincial frameworks (Ontario EDSTA, Manitoba Bill 51, Nova Scotia PIIDPA, BC FIPPA, Alberta PIPA), the OPC 2024-25 polling (88% concern), inferential extraction, and emotion-recognition validity.

**Chapter 11: IP & Copyright — The Canadian Contest, Honestly Presented.** The Canadian newspapers' lawsuit against OpenAI, the Geist/Craig vs TWUC/ACTRA academic-doctrinal disagreement on text-and-data mining, the CIGI likeness-rights argument and ACTRA NIL Rights converging on the same legal proposal from opposite directions, and the Beijing Treaty performer-rights question.

**Chapter 12: Film & Media — The Prompt Hits The Set.** Canadian film as both a real creative culture and a service-production machine, the tax-credit and CanCon architecture, COVID/strike/streaming aftershocks, indie production economics, Strange Harvest, Erica Lapadat Janzen's BC + AI soft-violence analysis, workflow substitution, likeness rights, and the working test for AI on set.

**Chapter 13: Misinformation & Deepfakes — What The Empirical Picture Actually Shows.** The 2025 Canadian election empirical study (5.9% deepfake rate, partisan asymmetry, 0.12% reach for harmful subset), the regulatory gap (Bill C-16 covers sexual deepfakes only), the Meta news block and its consequences, and the international comparison (EU AI Act, UK Online Safety Act, US TAKE IT DOWN Act).

**Chapter 14: Ethics, Bias & Fairness — The Question Is Not What You Think It Is.** The Lewis/Whaanga/Yolgörmez epistemology framing that organizes the chapter — bias is structural, not statistical. Documented Canadian cases, the algorithmic fairness literature and its limits, the corporate ethics-washing pattern, and the Abundant Intelligences constructive program.

**Chapter 15: Jobs & Economy — What The Evidence Shows, What The Disagreement Is About.** The 31%/29% Statistics Canada findings, the Acemoglu vs Autor academic disagreement on AI labour effects (presented as contested), the CUPE Senate Brief and the sectoral adoption pattern (information/cultural 35.6%, PSTS 31.7%, finance 30.6%), and the doubling Q2 2024 → Q2 2025 adoption trajectory.

**Part IV — Governance**

**Chapter 16: How AI Is Governed in Canada — The Actual Institutional Architecture.** The post-AIDA institutional reality, the sectoral pattern (Health Canada, OSFI, CRTC, OPC, CSA), the Voluntary Code of Conduct, the Treasury Board Directive on Automated Decision-Making, the provincial frameworks, the federalist constraint, and the comparative international landscape (EU AI Act, UK Online Safety Act, Council of Europe Framework Convention).

**Chapter 17: Transparency & Accountability — What You Can Know, What You Can't, And Why It Matters.** The Stanford FMTI 17-point decline as the centerpiece longitudinal evidence, the 22% Canadian data-centre PUE reporting rate, the corporate self-disclosure pattern, the absence of a Canadian facility-level data-centre census, and the EU EED Directive as the comparative standard.

**Part V — Path Forward**

**Chapter 18: Frameworks for Deciding — The Portable Toolkit.** The bias-mapping methodology as a complete framework, the seven working questions from the contested-questions chapters consolidated, the through-line analytical moves (three sovereignty layers, Jevons' paradox, the epistemology framing, the four-category actor map, the convergent transparency precondition), and worked examples.

**Chapter 19: What Canada Could Do — Specific Mechanisms For Closing The Gaps.** Concrete policy options the manual identifies without writing a manifesto — likeness rights (Denmark precedent), AI environmental disclosure (5-10 MW threshold), Indigenous data sovereignty federal commitment, Quebec Law 25 scaling, Bill C-16 expansion, mandatory data-centre reporting. Each with political coalition analysis.

**Chapter 20: Navigating the Conversation — What You Carry Forward.** Application of the toolkit to ongoing AI conversations — news, policy debate, workplace deployment, personal decisions, and the broader cultural conversation. The closing methodological synthesis.

**Source Library Appendix.** Detailed citations organized into ten sections by bias category: government documents, legislation, provincial grid operators, civil society, Indigenous-led frameworks, academic research, industry self-disclosure, international frameworks, litigation, and journalism.

## About the Author

**Alex Yesilcimen** is a Vancouver-based filmmaker, creative technologist, and digital creator working at the intersection of storytelling, emerging technology, and independent media. You might also know him as **Brin Shadewater**, the online identity he uses for his creative and commentary work.

Alex's background spans film production and computer science, and most of his projects live somewhere in that gap: cinematic work that asks hard questions about what the tools are doing, and technical work that stays rooted in story. As a Producer and Assistant Director, he's worked across countless productions over the last decade. His most recent feature producing credit is **Strange Harvest**, a theatrical horror film that, somewhat inadvertently, became a small case study in exactly the kind of AI panic this manual is trying to address.

**The Strange Harvest story belongs here.** During the film's festival run, the cut included roughly 30 seconds of licensed AI-generated stills, used as placeholders, legally, intentionally, and disclosed. The backlash was immediate and loud. Alex and his team made the call to remove the material for the theatrical release. What happened next is the part that stuck: the accusations didn't stop. The comment sections kept going, still claiming AI, still certain, now pointing at sequences that were entirely practical, or at visual quirks that were just questionable Photoshop work from a limited-budget production. People couldn't tell the difference. That experience sits underneath a lot of what this manual tries to do. The conversation about AI in creative work isn't just about what AI is actually doing. It's about the detection panic, the credibility collapse, and the way a label, once applied, becomes almost impossible to remove. Chapter 13 returns to this directly.

Alex is a member of the **Directors Guild of Canada** and a member of the **DGC AI Working Group**, which focuses on the ethical integration of AI and emerging technologies in the Canadian media industry: policy development, responsible adoption, and approaches that support workers rather than displace them. He is also a member of **Vancouver AI** and the broader **BC + AI Ecosystem**, the grassroots community centred on ethical, human-focused, cross-disciplinary approaches to AI and creativity that is one of this manual's most important intellectual homes.

**The computer thing started early.** Alex's first machine was a Macintosh LC II, and he grew up a committed Mac nerd — right up until about 2012, when Apple began soldering the RAM to the logic board and quietly retired the idea that you should be able to open, upgrade, and repair the thing you bought. At sixteen he was running a Hotline server and an adjacent internet radio station, which is a very specific way to learn how networks, communities, and bandwidth actually behave. He later spent about four years at Shaw Cable Systems (now Rogers) in Technical Services and Operations — internet, cable, and the launch of digital phone — and roughly five years in private security with firms including Reliance Protectron and ACME Security, both eventually absorbed by Telus. The throughline, then and now, is a stubborn set of commitments: free expression, net neutrality, and the belief that the people using a system deserve to understand and control it.

Through **Shadewater Labs**, his creative studio and experimental sandbox, Alex works on AI-assisted creative workflows, web development, automation systems, interactive storytelling, and emerging tools for filmmakers and independent creators. The studio is as much a way of thinking as it is a production entity: a place to break things, figure out what they actually do, and try to build something honest from the pieces.

Alex lives in Vancouver. He is diagnosed with ADHD and is on the autism spectrum — something worth naming here because a lot of this manual was written by a brain that works through hyperfocus, pattern recognition, and an inability to let a half-formed argument go unfinished. If the manual occasionally goes deeper than it needs to, that's probably why. If it also occasionally lands on something that a more conventionally organized process might have missed, that's probably why too.

### How to use this appendix

The guide has been promising at the end of every chapter that detailed citations appear here. This appendix delivers on that promise and does one more thing: it organizes sources by the bias categories the guide has been using throughout, so the appendix doubles as a worked example of the methodology in action. Readers can see how sources cluster by lean, verification status, and institutional position.

The appendix is organized into ten sections:

**A. Canadian Government — Strategy, Policy, and Operational Documents.** Federal framing, operational, and leaked documents. Lean: toward justifying current policy at the framing layer, lower lean at the operational layer.

**B. Canadian Legislation and Provincial Frameworks.** Federal and provincial statutes. Lean: institutional rather than advocacy-positioned, but the choice of what to legislate is itself political.

**C. Provincial Grid Operators and Utility Frameworks.** Operational disclosures from provincial electricity authorities. Lean: technical/operational rather than advocacy.

**D. Canadian Civil Society, Labour, and Advocacy.** Union, creator, civil-liberties, and public-interest organization documentation. Lean: toward the constituency the organization represents. Underlying evidence is often independently strong.

**E. Indigenous-led Frameworks and Research.** Primary frameworks and research from Indigenous-led organizations. The guide treats these as authoritative within their own frames and explicit about the guide's non-Indigenous-led status.

**F. Academic and Peer-Reviewed Research.** Journal articles, conference proceedings, peer-reviewed reports. Lean: toward what the discipline counts as rigour, which is itself a value commitment.

**G. Industry / Corporate Self-Disclosure.** Sustainability reports, technical disclosures, ethics frameworks, commissioned research. Lean: toward the company's interests, even when technically honest.

**H. International Frameworks and Foreign Legislation.** Treaties, foreign statutes, multilateral coordination instruments. Lean: institutional, but the choice of which to engage is policy.

**I. Litigation and Legal Cases.** Court filings and decisions. Lean: party-positioned in pleadings, more neutral in judicial reasoning.

**J. Investigative Journalism and Mainstream Press.** Reporting and analysis from journalism sources. Lean: toward the outlet's editorial position. Evidence often independently verifiable.

Within each section, entries are listed alphabetically by author or organization name. URLs are provided where stable and known; where a stable URL is not available, the entry indicates where the source can be located (publisher, archive, organizational website).

A few caveats on its limits. It is not exhaustive — sources cited in passing, where the citation wasn't load-bearing for the analysis, are not catalogued. It is not always current, since URLs, organizational structures, and document locations all change, so readers verifying a specific claim should be prepared to navigate to current versions. And it is not a substitute for the primary sources themselves; the guide's value is in helping readers read those sources more analytically, not in replacing them.

**Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual Performances (2012, WIPO).** International treaty extending moral rights to audiovisual performers. Canada has neither signed nor acceded; it is not among the contracting parties. Available at wipo.int. Relevant for the ACTRA performer-rights arguments.

**Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (May 2024).** First internationally-binding treaty on AI. **Canada signed February 11, 2025; ratification remains outstanding as of mid-2026 (the EU became the first ratifying party in May 2026; the treaty is not yet in force).** Available at coe.int.

**Denmark Copyright Act amendment on likeness rights (introduced 2025; pending final adoption as of mid-2026).** Draft legislation establishing likeness rights within copyright, with satire/parody/criticism-of-power exceptions and fifty-year post-mortem protection. The most developed legislative precedent for the convergent likeness-rights mechanism the guide identifies.

**European Union Artificial Intelligence Act.** Effective August 1, 2024, with phased implementation through 2026-2027. Available at eur-lex.europa.eu. The most-comprehensive AI regulatory framework currently in force globally. Risk-based classification, mandatory conformity assessment, fines up to 7% of global annual turnover (€35 million floor) for prohibited practices.

**European Union Digital Services Act.** Effective 2024. Available at eur-lex.europa.eu. Notice-and-action obligations for online platforms including AI-related content moderation transparency.

**European Union recast Energy Efficiency Directive (2023/1791) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364.** Mandatory reporting from EU data centres ≥500 kW installed IT power on PUE, WUE, key efficiency metrics, and waste heat recovery plans. Available at eur-lex.europa.eu.

**European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).** Available at eur-lex.europa.eu. Foundational data protection regulation with rights to be informed about automated decision-making and to explanation for consequential automated decisions.

**G7 Hiroshima AI Process documentation, including the International Code of Conduct for Advanced AI Developers.** October 2023. Available through G7 documentation and ised-isde.canada.ca. Multilateral AI governance coordination framework.

**Japan AI Strategy 2024 and AI Promotion Act.** Available through Japanese government policy documentation. Active regulatory engagement on AI governance.

**OECD AI Principles (2019, updated).** Available at oecd.org. Adopted by Canada and over 40 OECD member states. Non-binding but the most-cited international AI governance framework.

**Singapore PDPA and AI Governance Framework.** Available at pdpc.gov.sg. Coordinated approach with strong sectoral implementation.

**South Korea AI Basic Act and supporting framework.** Available through Korean government policy documentation.

**UK Online Safety Act (2023, in force with phasing through 2025-2026).** Available at gov.uk. Comprehensive online-harms regulation with Ofcom as regulator. Fines up to £18M or 10% of global annual revenue.

**US CHIPS and Science Act (2022).** US$52B subsidy for domestic semiconductor manufacturing. Available at commerce.gov.

**US TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025).** Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes On Websites and Networks Act. 48-hour platform removal requirement for non-consensual intimate images including AI-generated. Available through US Congress documentation.

**Various US state AI laws.** California AB 2839 (2024; political deepfake prohibitions around elections, successor to the sunset AB 730; preliminarily enjoined as unconstitutional in *Kohls v. Bonta* (2024), enforceability contested), Texas SB 751 (deepfake fraud provisions), Tennessee ELVIS Act (likeness protection), Illinois AI provisions, Colorado AI Act. Available through respective state legislative documentation.
